how_it_is_used: bie/brain/visual_thinking.py: the 'dikhane ki soch' step names, for every beat, its key idea, its relation (one of the ids below, or 'other' with a note, which is logged) and the things, people and places it names. The entry for the relation says how the relation is SHOWN; the things are shown as themselves (an icon or a picture found by code in the icon index and the asset library, never a word standing for the thing). Screen text is a name or a short natural phrase, never a sentence: the sentence lives in the narration and the subtitles (page-2 principle).
changes: 2026-10-31.1 (Task 046 Part D1): the first fourteen relations with how each is shown, from Navin's verdict of 30 October 2026.

relations.show: a cross mark on the thing refused (the thing's icon first, then the cross on it, on the word that refuses)

world.note: the refused thing as a label struck through

relations.show: a tick on the thing accepted
a law scroll with a stamp on it, beside the thing the law binds
a meter or a stack that fills up to a red line where it stops (the limit's number on the line)
two sizes side by side, or a crowd / stack that grows or shrinks on the word
a counted stack or crowd whose number is the narration's number
a numbered row or a timeline with arrows; the book's own years and labels when the part covers a book timeline
an arrow chain: the cause's icon, an arrow, the effect's icon or number
a split screen (the same slots on both sides) or a balance scale; the book's own table when the part covers one
a grouping: the whole as a box, its parts as icons inside it, or a tree
a map with the place marked, or the place's flag beside the thing
before and after side by side, the old struck out, the new in its place
a receipt or a handshake between the two parties, the promise's words as a short label
the thing asked about with a question mark beside it; the answer's picture replaces the mark when the answer comes
a relation outside this list: the step logs it (relations_outside_list) so Navin can add an entry; the beat still shows its things as themselves

picture_types.timeline: a book timeline (dated markers) drawn with the timeline_build block: the book's years and labels, nothing added
picture_types.gallery: a book panel of items (the six Evolution-of-Money pictures, the five currencies) drawn as a numbered row of icon cards: the thing's icon and its name under it
picture_types.table: a book table drawn as itself, row by row on the words that say the rows
picture_types.flow: a book flow (boxes joined by arrows) drawn with the flow_build block
picture_types.tree: a classification or structure drawn as a tree
picture_types.chart: numbers over years drawn as a chart
picture_types.map: a place drawn on a map (india_map, through the licence gate's map rule)
picture_types.things: the things themselves as icons, with the relation's mark, arrow, meter or scale

rules.rule: Every beat shows at least one non-text thing tied to its nouns or its relation (an icon, a mark, an arrow, a crowd or value step, a table row, a picture event; in a world a prop, a person, a price or a crowd step), cued on a word of that beat. A beat that only adds text is refused.

The screen never shows text alone for more than 10 seconds: while a beat is spoken, the thing it names is on screen (Navin, 30 October 2026: 'sirf text hi text screen par dikha to video ... ek book ban jaayegi').

Screen text is a name or a short natural phrase (at most 8 words; a board 2 lines of 28 characters), never a sentence: the sentence lives in the narration and the subtitles. The picture shows the thing itself, so its label is understood without reading (page-2 principle).

A book diagram or table the part covers is drawn as itself: a timeline with the book's years and labels, a table row by row, a panel of items as a gallery of icon cards, a flow as boxes and arrows. Code places it; the plan builds around it and never leaves it out.

A world (C) is used only when the beats are the story of the concept's real-world example with actors at a place, and that place comes from the example itself, never from a keyword of the narration; the same world kit is never used in two consecutive parts.
A caution, caveat or fact-check line ('illustrative numbers', 'imagined market', 'data not given', 'outside clarification') never appears on screen: it stays a background check in the records.
